study_type.claude: Experiment (controlled within-participant user study, with mixed methods)
study_type.note: Same design, different primary label: Claude leads with controlled experiment, NotebookLM with Mixed methods. Paper: within-participant setup with randomized tool order, plus Likert and qualitative responses.

research_method.claude: Controlled within-participant user study (randomized order; task types randomized between subjects): task correctness by test cases (linear model), user time from screen recordings/telemetry, post-study Likert (Wilcoxon signed-rank vs neutral), qualitative responses, exploratory trajectory analysis (153 annotated prompts)
research_method.nlm: Controlled within-subjects user study: task correctness and user effort measurements, 5-point Likert survey, qualitative trajectory and prompt analysis
research_method.value: Controlled within-participant user study comparing GitHub Copilot (copilot) and OpenHands (agent), tool order randomized, task types randomized between subjects (GAIA data analysis, SWE-Bench fix issue/add feature); task correctness via test cases, user effort time (screen recordings, event-stream telemetry), post-task 5-point Likert ratings, qualitative responses and interaction-trajectory analysis
research_method.note: Statistical tests (linear model, Wilcoxon signed-rank) and 153 annotated prompts reported only by Claude (not contradicted).

context.claude: Academic/lab; asynchronous study, 20 university-recruited students (regular Copilot users, no agent experience), realistic tasks in real OSS repositories (scikit-learn, astropy, matplotlib) and GAIA; April–May 2025
context.nlm: Academic/university; 20 students (regular Copilot users, novice agent users); realistic Python tasks in OSS repositories (matplotlib, scikit-learn) and GAIA data-analysis problems
context.value: academic; asynchronous user study with 20 university-recruited students (regular GitHub Copilot users, novice agent users; mostly 3–5 years programming experience) solving Python tasks from real OSS repositories (e.g., matplotlib, scikit-learn) and GAIA

space_applied.note: Claude: not mentioned; NotebookLM: referenced in related work.

ai_discussed.note: AI copilot vs autonomous coding agent is the object of study.

remote_covid.note: Both list work mode 'Remote' only because participants did the study asynchronously in their own time (one sentence on logistics); remote work is not a topic.

data_window.note: Claude: study conducted April–May 2025 (confirmed in text, 3.4 Procedure); NotebookLM gives no period.

cat_productivity.note: RQ1 productivity: task correctness rate and user effort (time); perceived speed also rated.

cat_quality.note: Borderline: NotebookLM labels task correctness 'Quality', but the paper defines it (task fully solved per test cases) as a productivity axis; no defect or code-quality metric.

cat_collaboration.note: Only human-AI interaction patterns; no human collaboration metric.

cat_satisfaction.note: Likert item on satisfaction (C5) comparing agent and copilot.

cat_activity.note: Claude tags interaction patterns 'Activity', but this is qualitative coding of prompts by workflow phase, not activity counts.

cat_devex.note: Cognitive load and flow rated as Likert items, but the DevEx framework is not cited or used.

cat_survey.note: Post-task 5-point Likert survey (cognitive load, new tasks, speed, flow, satisfaction, understanding) and open responses.

evidence.quote: We adopt a within-participant setup, where each participant interacts with both OpenHands and GitHub Copilot. We randomize the order in which participants interact with either.
For (2) and (3), we select tasks from SWE-Bench [23], which require users to fix issues by editing existing code files in a larger, real-world repository (e.g., matplotlib and scikit-learn).
We recruited a total of 20 students via university mailing lists.

we evaluate productivity along two complementary axes: task correctness, which captures whether the code satisfies all task specifications, and user effort, which reflects the amount of work a user puts in to achieve the correct solution.
we observe a 35% increase in task correctness when users have access to agents as compared to copilots
Interestingly, despite on average being able to solve more tasks correctly, participants were not necessarily more satisfied with agents.
In the post-task survey, we ask participants to rate their interactions with both the copilot and agent on a 5-point Likert scale from "strongly agree" to "strongly disagree".
